program:
## Athlete Interpretation

You have two equal top priorities for this block, not one. The first is driving the box squat in two directions at once, heavier top-end strength toward a bigger max, and real rep-strength work that moves you toward 180 kg for 10. The second is moving the one-arm pull-up from 2 strict reps toward 4 strict reps, which means keeping the work highly specific and not wasting elbow recovery on generic pulling that does not move that exact goal.

Your secondary goals fit if they are kept controlled. Strict overhead press can keep moving with two direct weekly exposures, as long as it stays behind the box squat and One-Arm Pull-up in the recovery queue. Aerobic work should help daily energy and mat recovery, not compete with them, so this block uses only low-fatigue Zone 2 work and avoids extra hard conditioning because your BJJ/MMA week already supplies plenty of high-intensity stress.

Your sport week is the main constraint. You have hard sessions on Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday, moderate sessions on Wednesday and Sunday, average recovery, and 6-7 hours of sleep. That means the gym has to be low volume, full-body across the week, and very selective. The box squat stays because it is clearly tolerated. Heavy RDLs and deep loaded squatting with lumbar flexion do not. Hip thrusts and chest-supported pulling stay in because they give you useful return without unnecessary spinal fatigue.

This block also respects what you explicitly do not want. Freestanding Handstand Push-up does not get its own working slot here. It is a nice extra, but right now it should not take recovery away from box squat, one-arm pull-up, overhead press, conditioning, or mat performance.

## Key Programming Priorities

This block is built around four priorities.

1. Box squat gets two direct weekly exposures.
 One session is heavy and specific for top-end strength. One session is moderate-load rep work for parallel box squat strength-endurance. That is the cleanest way to serve both outcomes you named without forcing too much lower-body fatigue into a hard mat week.

2. One-arm pull-up gets two direct weekly exposures.
 You already own 2 strict reps, so this block does not waste time making eccentrics the main event. One exposure is strict one-arm singles and clusters. The second is lightly assisted one-arm pulling for more high-quality unilateral volume.

3. Overhead press keeps progressing, but behind the two main priorities.
 You will press twice per week, one heavier day and one slightly higher-rep day. That is enough to move it forward without letting it steal from One-Arm Pull-up elbows, shoulders, or recovery.

4. Conditioning stays easy and useful.
 You asked for better aerobic conditioning and better day-to-day energy without hurting strength or BJJ/MMA. The answer here is repeated easy bike or rower work, not extra intervals.

The weekly structure is full-body because your sport load is high. That gives better frequency per goal and spreads soreness and fatigue more evenly than a body-part split would.

## Method Selection and Microcycle Logic

We are using a sport-aware daily undulating structure inside a full-body week.

In plain terms, the same main goals come back more than once each week, but each exposure has a different job:
- one heavy box squat day
- one rep-strength box squat day
- one strict One-Arm Pull-up day
- one assisted One-Arm Pull-up day
- one heavier OHP day
- one volume OHP day

That setup fits you better than a pure specialization block on one lift because your two main goals can coexist, as long as weekly fatigue stays tight and the sport week stays the boss.

The day placement is deliberate.

Monday is a controlled lower and upper-support day before hard mat work. It carries the box squat rep-strength slot because the lift is tolerated, the load is moderate, and it gives you enough time to recover before the heavy box squat on Friday.

Wednesday is the cleanest place for the second One-Arm Pull-up exposure and the heavier overhead press work because the sport session is moderate, not hard. That gives you a better chance of getting useful quality from both patterns.

Friday is the clearest high-quality strength day of the week. No listed sport session, enough distance from Thursday hard work, and a full recovery runway into Saturday. That is where the strict One-Arm Pull-up work and heavy box squat go.

Saturday is upper-body volume and aerobic support. It lets the press get its second exposure, gives you more upper-back work, and builds aerobic recovery without beating up your lower back before the next hard sequence of mat days.

Low-fatigue explosive work stays in as med ball throws. That gives you a fast output stimulus without the fatigue cost of more loaded speed work.

## Weeks 2-4 Progression Map

Weeks 2-4 are built to progress by small changes, not by trying to force breakthroughs every session.

Week 2
- Add a little more total work to the main patterns if Week 1 is clean.
- Box squat heavy and rep day both add one work set.
- Strict One-Arm Pull-up adds one more single per side.
- Assisted One-Arm Pull-up adds one set.
- Heavy OHP adds one set.
- Zone 2 extends slightly.

Week 3
- Shift from volume toward slightly higher intensity on the main strength slots.
- Heavy box squat drops reps and gets heavier.
- Rep box squat gets slightly heavier and drops to sets of 5.
- Strict One-Arm Pull-up moves to short clusters.
- Assisted One-Arm Pull-up moves from doubles toward triples if assistance stays light and reps stay strict.
- Heavy OHP drops to sets of 3 with a higher load.

Week 4
- Consolidate, do not coast.
- Keep the same exercise structure.
- Hold or slightly trim set count while keeping the heavier work honest and clean.
- The goal is to leave the block with sharper reps, better bar speed, and better unilateral pulling quality, not to bury yourself in a forced deload.

Back-off trigger during the block
If box squat bar speed clearly drops for more than one exposure in a row, if strict One-Arm Pull-up singles start turning into grinders, if elbows or lower back stay more irritated the next day than usual, or if mat sharpness drops across the week, hold the next week's load and cut one set from the offending lift before changing anything else.

## Loading Rules and Calibration

Box squat loads are anchored to your current confirmed ability, not to the goal numbers. For this block I am treating 210 kg as the working max reference for box squat loading. That gives you realistic heavy ranges without overshooting.

Overhead press loads are based on your current 75 kg for 4-5 and your historical 90 kg max, so the press ranges in the sheet are estimates built from your current level, not from the 100 kg goal.

For the main lifts:
- Use the low end of the range on a flatter recovery day
- Move toward the top end only if your warm-up speed is honest and the target RIR is still there
- If the first work set is clearly heavier than planned, stay in the bottom half of the range and do not force the top end

For One-Arm Pull-up work:
- Strict day means clean singles only
- Stop a set the moment you need body English, rotation, or a softer lockout
- Assisted day means the lightest help that still gives you strict reps
- The point is quality unilateral pulling volume, not forcing ugly reps

For med ball work:
- Every rep should look fast
- Stop before any visible drop in pop or timing

For accessories:
- Work mostly in the RPE 7-8 range
- Leave a little room
- Nothing on this block needs junk fatigue

## GPP and Conditioning Prescription

Conditioning stays low impact and aerobic.

You asked to improve aerobic conditioning and day-to-day energy without reducing strength or BJJ/MMA performance. With your current mat schedule, the highest-value answer is Zone 2 work on the bike or rower. That gives you recovery support, better between-session energy, and better aerobic base without creating extra soreness or extra CNS load.

This block uses 2 dedicated Zone 2 exposures per week.
- Wednesday, 15-20 minutes
- Saturday, 20-25 minutes

Intensity target:
- conversational pace
- nasal breathing if comfortable
- you finish feeling better than when you started, not flattened

What is intentionally not included:
- no extra hard intervals
- no hard running
- no threshold work
- no random circuits

Your hard conditioning already comes from BJJ/MMA. The gym should fill the aerobic gap, not duplicate the hard work you already do.

## Pain Gate and Substitutions

For your lower back, the rule is simple. Keep the squat pattern on the exact box squat setup that you already know is tolerated, and avoid deep loaded squatting with lumbar flexion and heavy RDL loading that has already shown a tendency to flare you.

That is why this block uses:
- box squat to parallel as the main squat
- hip thrust as the main posterior-chain assistance
- chest-supported rowing instead of heavy unsupported rows
- med ball throws for explosive maintenance instead of more loaded spinal work

If lower back sensitivity is higher than normal on a given day:
- keep the box height exactly where it is
- stay at the low end of the prescribed load range
- cut one set before you cut the whole session
- swap hip thrust for a lighter glute bridge if needed

If One-Arm Pull-up elbows or forearms start getting more irritated than usual:
- keep the strict day to singles only
- reduce assistance-day volume first
- use neutral-grip bilateral pulling only as support, not as a replacement for the skill unless the unilateral work clearly stops being tolerable

If shoulder tolerance is off on press day:
- first swap the heavy standing press to a landmine press or neutral-grip dumbbell press
- keep the same basic weekly structure
- do not replace OHP with Handstand Push-up work

Freestanding Handstand Push-up remains deprioritized this block. If you feel great and want to touch the position, keep it to a very short warm-up balance touch only, never enough to affect pressing or mat quality.

## Exercise Reasoning

The standout choices here are all about return per unit of fatigue.

Box squat to parallel is the central lower-body choice because it directly matches your main goal and your tolerance profile. There is no reason to chase a lower-cost but less specific squat when this exact pattern is both useful and tolerated.

Hip thrust is the main posterior-chain assistance because you specifically tolerate it well and it lets us keep glute and lockout strength work in the week without paying the spinal cost of heavy RDLs.

Strict One-Arm Pull-up singles and lightly assisted One-Arm Pull-up doubles are the right pair because you already own 2 strict reps. The strict day keeps the real skill in the week. The assisted day lets you accumulate more specific unilateral volume without turning every set into a max attempt.

Overhead press is split into one heavier and one slightly higher-rep day because that keeps it moving without forcing a third pressing exposure. That is enough for progress and still leaves recovery available for the main priorities.

Med ball throws are in because you wanted low-fatigue explosive work kept alive. They give you that without stealing from box squat or mat work.

Chest-supported rowing, face pulls, and cable laterals are all there because they preserve upper-back and delt work with very little fatigue cost, and because you explicitly wanted lateral raises and face pulls kept in.

## Safety, Recovery, and Lifestyle Notes

Your biggest performance limiter on this block will not be motivation. It will be whether recovery stays predictable enough for the week to repeat.

The three things that matter most:
1. Sleep. With 6-7 hours, you are right on the line where extra gym fatigue becomes expensive. If you can get even 30-45 more minutes on the nights before Wednesday and Friday sessions, that will help.
2. Fueling between gym and mat work. On days where the gym comes 6 hours before BJJ/MMA, eat a real meal with protein and carbs in the gap. Do not let the second session run on fumes.
3. Honesty on rep quality. Your main lifts on this block are effective only if you stop before technique drifts.

Watch points:
- lower back that stays tighter than usual into the next morning
- One-Arm Pull-up reps that start rotating or getting sticky
- shoulders that lose overhead line rather than just feeling worked
- mat sessions that feel flat across more than one day

If any of those show up more than once in a week, report them. That is a program adjustment signal, not something to grind through blindly.

## Client Action Steps

1. Run the week exactly as written before judging it.
2. On every box squat set, log the actual load you used inside the range and whether the last rep still matched the target RIR.
3. On strict One-Arm Pull-up day, log whether every rep was truly strict, side by side.
4. On assisted One-Arm Pull-up day, log what assistance let you keep perfect reps.
5. After each Zone 2 session, note whether you finished feeling better, same, or worse than when you started.
6. Tell me immediately if lower back symptoms start lingering into the next day, or if One-Arm Pull-up elbow tolerance changes.
7. At the end of Week 1, report back with four things only: box squat loads used, One-Arm Pull-up quality, OHP quality, and whether Wednesday or Saturday Zone 2 noticeably improved day-to-day energy.
